vignette:
He was eighteen, a first-year student at a university in a city that felt vast and promising. She was a classmate from his UX design course, someone he had helped a few times with Figma layouts. That was all. Within weeks, her messages multiplied - first on the class group, then private DMs, then texts, then calls at 2 a.m. He asked her to stop. She didn't. She began waiting for him outside the design studio, sitting two rows behind him in lectures, appearing at the coffee shop he visited every morning. He changed his routine. She seemed to know it anyway. He moved dorm rooms. She left a note under his new door. The university's security office said they couldn't do much unless she threatened him. She never did. She only watched.

For six months he lived in a state of low, constant dread. His grades slipped. He stopped using the campus app to check his schedule. He wore headphones even when listening to nothing, so he wouldn't have to hear footsteps behind him. The police finally got involved when she followed him onto a bus and sat directly beside him, despite empty seats. A restraining order was issued. She transferred schools. He has not seen her in a year.

Now he is nineteen. He still works as a UX designer, a role he landed through a paid internship that turned full-time. In theory, the job is perfect - he designs interfaces that feel intuitive and safe. But in practice, his office is an open-plan floor, and someone is always walking behind his desk. He cannot focus. He hears her presence in the creak of every chair, every soft cough. He keeps his laptop screen angled away from the aisle. When a colleague approaches from behind, he flinches. Once, he accidentally knocked over his coffee. Now he works from home three days a week, and even there he sits with his back to a wall, his phone face-up and buzzing.

His PCL-5 score is 65. In the sessions, he speaks of the stalking as if it were ongoing. He replays the moments when she appeared - the way she would tilt her head and smile, as though his fear was a private joke. He has nightmares of being followed through endless, identical corridors. He wakes sweating, heart hammering, and checks the locks on his apartment door twice. He avoids the coffee shop near his old university. He deleted all social media accounts. He bought a new phone number, but still feels a phantom vibration in his pocket.

He does not date. The thought of someone taking an interest in him, even kindly, sends a current of cold fear through his chest. He has told his parents back home (they live in Ghana) that everything is fine. He cannot bring himself to explain why he is so tired all the time, why he has stopped answering video calls. His boss has noticed the drop in productivity. The project he is leading - a health app for people with chronic anxiety - is behind schedule. He sits in front of his wireframes, the cursor blinking, and thinks: She is still out there. She knows my name. She knows where I work. He has started taking different routes home, even though he knows it makes no sense. The past tense has not become the past. It is, for him, still unfolding.
